title: Osho and the Zen Stories That Wake You Up
description: What Osho taught about Zen, in plain words. Five old Zen stories, told slowly, each one a small bucket of cold water. The master who only said: Is that so? Two monks and a woman at the river. The stonecutter who wanted to be everything. A samurai who asked about heaven and hell. A nun whose bucket broke under the full moon. And the finger pointing at the moon. Then we sit with the sound of a temple bell.

chapters.title: Osho and the Zen Stories That Wake You Up

beats.say: Osho told hundreds of Zen stories, and they are strange. They don't give you a philosophy to carry home. They hit you... like a bucket of cold water in the morning.
And if you are lucky, for one moment you are awake. The mind stops, it doesn't know what to say... and in that gap, something opens.

He gave this advice: "Remain in wonder if you want mysteries to open up for you." So don't try to solve these stories, like a puzzle in the newspaper. Just let them fall into you, like stones into a pond.
And watch the ripples. The ripples are the real teaching.
In a village in Japan lived a master named Hakuin. Everybody respected him. They said: what a pure man, what a holy man.
Then a young girl in the village became pregnant. Her parents were furious. Who is the father? And the girl, afraid, said: it is Hakuin.
The parents ran to the master's hut, shouting and abusing him. And Hakuin listened, and said only this: Is that so?
When the child was born, they brought it to him. You are the father, you look after it. He took the baby in his arms and said: Is that so?
His good name was finished. Nobody came to him any more. But he cared for the child with great love. He begged for milk from house to house.
A year later the girl could not bear it. She told the truth. The real father was a young man who worked in the fish market.
The parents ran to Hakuin again, begging his forgiveness, asking for the child back. And he gave the child, and said: Is that so?
This is what Osho called being centred. Praise came, blame came, and he remained the same. Like a mirror, which shows whatever comes, and keeps nothing.
Two monks were walking back to their monastery. They came to a river, swollen after the rain. At the bank stood a young woman, afraid to step into the water.
The older monk simply picked her up, carried her across the water, and put her down on the other side. Then the two monks walked on.
The younger monk was boiling inside. For hours he said nothing. Finally, at the gate of the monastery, he burst out: We are monks! We are not even allowed to look at a woman. How could you carry her?
And the old monk said: Brother, I put her down at the river. You are still carrying her.
Look at your own mind. How many people are you still carrying? The man who insulted you ten years ago. The woman who left. The father who never understood.
Osho taught: die to the past every moment. They have gone long ago. Only you are carrying them, mile after mile. Put them down at the river.

chapters.title: The Finger Pointing at the Moon

beats.say: There is an old Zen saying. The teaching is like a finger pointing at the moon. Look at the moon... not at the finger.
But what do people do? They fall in love with the finger. They worship the finger. They fight about whose finger is the true finger.
The temples, the books, the words of the masters... even these words tonight. All fingers. Useful, beautiful... but only fingers.
And the moon is shining all the time, above your head, waiting for you to look up.
Osho taught: words are only fingers. Don't hold on to them. Use them... and throw them away. Look where they are pointing.

chapters.title: The Stonecutter
chapters.ref: A Japanese folk tale · Osho, The Book of Wisdom

beats.say: There was a poor stonecutter who worked all day at the foot of a mountain. One day a rich merchant passed by in a beautiful carriage, and he thought: if only I were rich.
And a voice from the mountain said: so be it. He became the rich merchant. Then the prince came by with soldiers and drums, and everybody bowed. If only I were the prince.
He became the prince. But the sun burned him in his golden chair, and he thought: the sun is more powerful. And he became the sun.
Then a cloud covered the sun, and he became the cloud. Then the wind blew the cloud away, and he became the wind.
But the wind could not move the mountain. The mountain is the most powerful, he thought. And he became the mountain.
And then he felt something chipping, chipping at his feet. He looked down. It was a poor stonecutter, working at the foot of the mountain.
Osho said: "Be — don't try to become." Ambition is a wheel. It goes round and round, and brings you back to where you started... only more tired.
A great samurai came to an old Zen master and said: Tell me, old man, is there really a heaven and a hell?
The master looked at him and laughed. You, a samurai? You look more like a beggar. And your sword is so blunt it could not cut a radish.
The samurai turned red with rage. He pulled out his sword and raised it to strike the old man down.
And quietly the master said: Here open the gates of hell.
The samurai froze. He understood. Slowly he put the sword back, and bowed down to the old man, full of gratitude. And the master said: Here open the gates of heaven.
Osho taught that heaven and hell are not places. They are not after death. They are moments, and you are choosing between them... a hundred times every day.

chapters.title: No Water, No Moon
chapters.ref: A Zen story · Osho, No Water, No Moon

beats.say: A nun named Chiyono studied for years, and nothing happened. Then one night she was carrying an old wooden bucket full of water.
In the water she could see the full moon shining. She walked carefully, looking at the moon in her bucket.
Suddenly the bamboo strip holding the bucket together snapped. The bottom fell out. The water was gone... and the moon in the water was gone.
And in that moment Chiyono was free. No water, no moon. All the reflections she had been holding were gone, and only the real moon remained, shining in the sky.
Osho named a whole book after this story: No Water, No Moon. Your bucket is your mind. One day the bottom falls out... and that is not a loss. That is the beginning.
Why do the masters tell stories? Why not simply say the truth, plainly, in one sentence, and finish the matter?
Because the mind is a clever guard at the gate. Give it a sentence, and it argues. Give it a philosophy, and it collects it, like stamps in an album.
But a story slips past the guard. The mind thinks: oh, it is only a little story, for children. And while it is laughing, the story goes straight into the heart.
That is why Osho told so many stories. Years later, on some ordinary afternoon, one suddenly opens inside you like a flower. And you laugh, because now you understand.

chapters.title: A Meditation: The Sound of the Bell

beats.say: Now let us sit. Osho taught that silence is the real teaching of Zen. Close your eyes. Imagine that somewhere far away, in a temple on a hill, a bell is being struck.
Listen to the sound. It is loud at first... and then it begins to fade. Go with it. Follow the sound as it becomes softer, and softer.
Where does the sound go? It goes into silence. Go with it... into the silence.
Now the bell rings again. And again it fades. Each time, let yourself go a little deeper into what remains when the sound is gone.
There is no need to think about it. No need to understand it. Just listen to the silence, the way you listened to the bell.
The silence was here before the bell. It will be here after the bell. It is here now. You are this silence.
Rest in it. Nothing to do. Just this... and this.
And now, take a deep breath. Slowly open your eyes. Carry the sound of the bell with you... and the silence behind it.
